claims.text: HEA nanoparticle structural and chemical stability is governed by the balance between configurational entropy and lattice-distortion energy.
Greater atomic-size mismatch produces higher lattice-distortion energy.
Nanoparticles with greater atomic-size mismatch are more likely to undergo elemental segregation at elevated temperatures.
Nanoparticles with greater atomic-size mismatch are more likely to undergo phase separation at elevated temperatures.
The initial nanoparticles are homogeneous, single-phase solid solutions containing five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios.
Selecting constituent metals with minimized versus maximized atomic-size differences provides a controlled comparison of lattice distortion.
Thermal cycling will span 473–1923 K under controlled catalytic or thermoelectric atmospheres.
Atomic-size mismatch among the constituent elements induces lattice-distortion energy.
When lattice-distortion energy exceeds the stabilizing effect of configurational entropy, local strain drives segregation of constituent metals.
Strain-induced elemental segregation leads to phase separation or chemical inhomogeneity.
Particles with lower lattice distortion remain stable single phases.
After thermal cycling, the larger-size-mismatch group will exhibit secondary-phase formation or elemental segregation.
After thermal cycling, the minimized-size-mismatch group will largely retain its initial single-phase structure.
The proposed relationship applies up to 1923 K when the environment does not impose extreme additional chemical driving forces.
Retention of homogeneous single-phase structures by both comparison groups without observable segregation or phase separation would falsify the proposed governing role of atomic-size mismatch.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis requires atomic-size mismatch to be the only variable, but minimizing versus maximizing mismatch by selecting different constituent metals also changes elemental identity and associated chemical, thermodynamic, kinetic, and surface properties.
